facts.statement: Amargatitanis is a dicraeosaurid sauropod dinosaur from the Barremian-aged La Amarga Formation in Neuquén, Argentina.
facts.quote: Amargatitanis (meaning "Amarga giant") is a genus of dicraeosaurid sauropod dinosaur (a type of large, long-necked quadrupedal herbivorous dinosaur) from the Barremian-aged (Lower Cretaceous) La Amarga Formation of Neuquén, Argentina.

facts.statement: Argentine paleontologist José Bonaparte unearthed the remains in 1983, and they were later described as Amargatitanis macni by Sebastián Apesteguía.
facts.quote: These remains were unearthed by Argentine paleontologist José Bonaparte in 1983 during an expedition by the Museo Argentino de Ciencias Naturales and later described as a new genus and species, Amargatitanis macni by Sebastián Apesteguía.

facts.statement: The genus name Amargatitanis combines "Amarga," the location of the fossils, and "titanis," meaning "titan."
facts.quote: The genus name comes from the words Amarga, where the fossils were collected, and titanis meaning "titan".

facts.statement: The species name macni honors the Museo Argentino de Ciencias Naturales (MACN), where the fossils are stored.
facts.quote: Its species name is in reference to the MACN (Museo Argentino de Ciencias Naturales), where the remains are stored.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen was cataloged under the number MACN PV N53 at the Museo Argentino de Ciencias Naturales.
facts.quote: These remains were taken to the Museo Argentino de Ciencias Naturales where they were cataloged under the specimen number MACN PV N53.

facts.statement: The skeleton remained undescribed until 2007, when it was named Amargatitanis macni by Sebastián Apesteguía.
facts.quote: The skeleton remained undescribed until 2007, when Argentine researcher Sebastián Apesteguía named it Amargatitanis macni.

facts.statement: Sebastián Apesteguía erroneously assigned a scapula and six caudal vertebrae found in 1986 to the specimen, despite them coming from different rock layers.
facts.quote: Apesteguía erroneously assigned a scapula (MACN PV N34) and six caudal vertebrae (MACN PV N51) to the specimen, despite coming from other rock layers and being found in 1986.

facts.statement: Originally assigned to Titanosauria, a 2016 reanalysis demonstrated that Amargatitanis is a dicraeosaurid dipolodocoid.
facts.quote: It was originally assigned to the group Titanosauria due to the anatomy of the scapula and caudal vertebra, but a 2016 reanalysis of the holotype (MACN PV N53) fossils demonstrated that Amargatitanis was instead a dicraeosaurid dipolodocoid.

facts.statement: Amargatitanis lived approximately 129 to 123 million years ago in the Barremian-aged Puesto Antigual Member of the La Amarga Formation.
facts.quote: Amargatitanis macni is known from a single specimen, the holotype MACN PV N53, which was found in the Barremian-aged Puesto Antigual Member of the La Amarga Formation, approximately 129 to 123 million years old.

facts.statement: One estimate suggests Amargatitanis reached around 12 meters (39.7 feet) in length and weighed 3.5 metric tons.
facts.quote: It reached around 12 meters (39.7 feet) long and 3.5 MT according to one estimate.

facts.statement: As a dicraeosaurid, Amargatitanis likely resembled Dicraeosaurus and Amargasaurus, featuring shorter necks and long neural spines extending from the neck and trunk vertebrae.
facts.quote: As a dicraeosaurid, Amargatitanis would have resembled better known members of the family such as Dicraeosaurus and Amargasaurus, which had shorter necks than most other sauropods and long neural spines extending from the vertebrae of the neck and trunk.

facts.statement: One study estimated Amargatitanis's mass at 11.406 metric tons, slightly larger than the estimate for Amargasaurus in the same study.
facts.quote: It was a small sauropod, with one study estimating its mass at 11.406 MT, slightly larger than the same study's estimate for Amargasaurus of 10.195 MT.

facts.statement: The femur of Amargatitanis is distinctive because it is much wider at the upper end than the lower end, unlike other sauropods where the ends are approximately equal in width.
facts.quote: The femur is distinctive in that it is much wider at its proximal (upper) end than at its distal (lower) end, whereas in other sauropods, including Dicraeosaurus, both ends are approximately equal in width.

facts.statement: The tibia of Amargatitanis has a low cnemial crest, similar to Dicraeosaurus and Amargasaurus, unlike the higher crest found in most macronarians.
facts.quote: The tibia has a low cnemial crest, similar to that of Dicraeosaurus and Amargasaurus and unlike the higher cnemial crest found in most macronarians.

facts.statement: In 2022, Guillermo Windholz and colleagues argued that Amargatitanis was especially closely related to Pilmatueia and Bajadasaurus within a South American dicraeosaurid clade.
facts.quote: In 2022, researcher Guillermo Windholz and colleagues argued that South American dicraeosaurids formed a clade based on their biogeography and results of phylogenetic analyses, with Amargatitanis being especially closely related to Pilmatueia and Bajadasaurus.

facts.statement: Amargatitanis fossils were discovered in 1983 in the La Amarga Formation by José Fernando Bonaparte.
facts.quote: La descripción está basado en los especímenes MACN PV N51, 53, y 34, los cuales fueron descubiertos en 1983, en la Formación La Amarga por José Fernando Bonaparte

facts.statement: The known fossil remains of Amargatitanis include six tail vertebrae, a femur, a scapula, and an astragalus.
facts.quote: Estos restos fósiles consistían en seis vértebras caudales, un fémur, una escápula y un astrágalo.

facts.statement: The formal description of Amargatitanis was published in 2007 by the Argentine paleontologist Sebastián Apesteguía.
facts.quote: La descripción formal se llevó a cabo en el 2007 por el paleontólogo argentino Sebastián Apesteguía.

facts.statement: Researchers debated whether Amargatitanis was a titanosaurian, noting that its holotype and syntypes were found in different locations and lacked valid titanosaurian characteristics.
facts.quote: Aunque fue clasifica en principio como un titanosaurio, dicha clasificación de Amargatitanis fue puesta en duda posteriormente por otros autores, quienes señalaron que una escápula (MACM PV N34) y seis vértebras de la cola (MACN PV N51), consideradas como sintipos de Amargatitanis fueron halladas en localidades diferentes a MACN PV N53 y que las supuestas características de titanosaurio del género no eran válidas.

facts.statement: A 2016 re-evaluation by Pablo Ariel Gallina reclassified Amargatitanis as a dicraeosaurid.
facts.quote: Una revaluación publicada en 2016 por Pablo Ariel Gallina reclasificó a Amargatitanis como un dicreosáurido.

facts.statement: Amargatitanis lived approximately 130 million years ago during the Early Cretaceous Barremian stage in what is now South America.
facts.quote: que vivió a principios del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 130 millones de años, en el Barremiense, en lo que hoy es Sudamérica.

facts.statement: Amargatitanis fossils come from the La Amarga Formation in the Neuquén Basin, dating to the Barremian and late Aptian of the Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Amargatitanis stems from sedimentary rocks of the La Amarga Formation, which is part of the Neuquén Basin and dates to the Barremian and late Aptian of the Early Cretaceous.

facts.statement: Evidence from neck and inner ear anatomy suggests Amargatitanis fed at heights of up to 2.7 meters.
facts.quote: Amargatitanis and Amargasaurus probably fed above ground level at heights of up to 2.7 m, as evidenced by the anatomy of their neck and inner ear.

facts.statement: Analysis of growth marks in a femur indicates that the Amargatitanis specimen was at least 19 years old when it died.
facts.quote: The femur of Amargatitanis bears 19 cyclical growth marks, indicating that the individual was at least 19 years old at the time of death.

facts.statement: The unusually high number of growth marks in Amargatitanis suggests that some sauropods may have grown discontinuously rather than continuously.
facts.quote: The high number of cyclical growth marks seen in Amargatitanis is unusual for sauropods, and possibly indicates that some sauropods grew discontinuously rather than continuously.

facts.statement: Amargatitanis is classified within the family Dicraeosauridae.
facts.quote: familia: Dicraeosauridae

facts.statement: The parent group of the genus Amargatitanis is the family Dicraeosauridae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Dicraeosauridae

facts.statement: Amargatitanis lived between 125.77 and 121.4 million years ago during the Barremian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Barremian to Barremian (125.77 to 121.4 million years ago)
